---
title: "Quiz: acceptor photobleaching"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $E = 1 - I_D^\text{pre}/I_D^\text{post}$ (donor before and after bleaching the acceptor).

---

**Q1.** Why does the donor get brighter when the acceptor is destroyed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where did the donor's missing light go before?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With the acceptor present, a fraction $E$ of the donor's excitations is transferred to it instead of being emitted by the donor. Without acceptor nothing takes that energy, so the donor emits it: it is dequenched.
:::

---

**Q2.** The donor in the bleached region goes from 450 to 600. What is $E$? What should a region outside the bleached area give?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$1 - \text{pre}/\text{post}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$E = 1 - 450/600 = 0.25$. Outside the region the acceptor is intact: the donor should not change, and $E$ should be 0 (apart from noise and donor bleaching).
:::

---

**Q3.** Only 80 % of the acceptor was bleached, and the observed $E$ is 0.20. Is the true $E$ higher or lower? Compute it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$E = E_\text{obs}/(b + (1 - b)E_\text{obs})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Higher: the remaining acceptors still quench their donors. $E = 0.20/(0.8 + 0.2\cdot0.2) = 0.20/0.84 = 0.238$.
:::

---

**Q4.** A region outside the bleach box, in the same cell, lost 10 % of its donor signal during the experiment. What does this do to $E$ if you do not correct it? How do you correct it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of pre and post is affected?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The donor bleached by itself, so the post image is too dim and $E$ comes out too low (possibly negative outside the box). Correct by dividing the post values by 0.90 (the control's after/before ratio) before computing $1 - \text{pre}/\text{post}$.
:::

---

**Q5.** The $E$ map shows a bright crescent on one side of every cell and a dark one on the other. What happened?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the cell outlines before and after.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The cells moved (or the stage drifted) between the before and after images: at the leading edge the post image has signal where pre had little, and vice versa. Align the images before dividing.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why is acceptor photobleaching called an end-point method, and why is it hard in living cells?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is left after the measurement?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The acceptor is destroyed, so the measurement can be done once per cell, not repeated over time. In living cells bleaching takes time, during which unbleached acceptors diffuse into the region (and molecules move), so the dequenching is underestimated.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two samples both give $E_\text{app} = 0.2$. In one, all donors are bound at $E = 0.2$; in the other, half are bound at $E = 0.4$. Can acceptor bleaching tell them apart? What can?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Intensities add.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: every intensity method measures $fE$, 0.2 in both. The donor's lifetime decay can: one lifetime in the first sample, two (unquenched and $\tau_D(1 - 0.4)$) in the second.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that for Poisson counts $P$ (before) and $Q$ (after), $\sigma_E \approx (P/Q)\sqrt{1/P + 1/Q}$, and evaluate it for $P = 600$, $Q = 800$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Linearise $1 - P/Q$; the variance of each count equals its mean.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\delta E = -\delta P/Q + P\,\delta Q/Q^2$, so $\sigma_E^2 = P/Q^2 + P^2 Q/Q^4 = (P/Q)^2(1/P + 1/Q)$. For 600/800: $0.75\sqrt{1/600 + 1/800} = 0.0405$.
:::
